text:
Education in Sweden is a comprehensive, nine-year compulsory system (grundskola) from ages 6–16, structured into three stages: lower (grades 1–3), middle (grades 4–6), and upper (grades 7–9). Students take 16 compulsory subjects, including Swedish, mathematics, physical education, English, and arts, with a foreign language course available from grade 6. A grading system uses letters (A–E) and a numerical total (up to 340) for university applications, with a national test administered in grades 3, 6, and 9.
Upper secondary education (gymnasieskola) lasts three years and includes 18 national programs—15 preparatory and 3 vocational—offering pathways to university. Students must pass 8–12 subjects, including core subjects, to qualify. A diploma project is required in all programs.
Higher education includes public universities and university colleges offering degrees aligned with the Bologna Process (bachelor’s, master’s, PhD). Degrees are awarded in three cycles: basic (180 credits), advanced (120 credits), and doctoral (240 credits). Public institutions offer free education for EU/EEA/Swiss citizens, with financial aid available. Independent schools (friskolor), funded by municipalities, are common and provide private alternatives, though their grading and standards have drawn criticism.
The system emphasizes equity, with policies promoting inclusion, anti-discrimination, and quality assurance. PISA and PIRLS results show strong performance in reading and mathematics, though recent concerns have been raised about declining test scores and grading practices.
